unit_label: CB Module A unit 3: contemporary issues in central banking

facts.statement: Autonomy and independence of a central bank (courseware): in the initial years central banks were established as private institutions and remained independent of government control; this continued till the outbreak of the Second World War; later the functional role of central banks widened. Around the Second World War central banks in a number of countries (Germany, France, England, Japan, Italy and Sweden) were made subordinate to their governments; recent experience has revealed that central banks can best pursue their goals in a climate of independence; it was also realised that it is possible to attain and sustain a low level of inflation if the central bank functions as an autonomous institution. The revival of interest in central bank independence can be attributed to several factors: the reforms in centrally planned economies, the establishment of a new European Central Bank (ECB) and the importance of price stability in a world characterised by substantial cross border financial flows; to achieve the set goals central banks should ideally enjoy both operational independence and legal independence. The rationale: central banks free from government control and endowed with constitutional assurance towards autonomy could perform their responsibilities best, not only in terms of pursuing goals in the long-term interest but also in terms of managing short-term issues relating to public debt in line with set goals; the higher the level of support that the central bank provides to government, the greater would be the intensity of pressure in managing short-term liquidity; autonomy shields the bank from such fiscal pressures. Arguments for independence: political systems behave myopically, drifting towards inflationary policies guided by short-run benefits and overlooking the long-run costs; an independent central bank, given the responsibility of price stability, would be in a better position to incorporate the broader economic policy objectives for monetary policy formulation. In recent years a number of central banks started pursuing an independent monetary policy: the Bank of England was legally made an independent body in June 1998 (though it had enjoyed substantial independence during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries); the Bank of Japan gained operational independence in April 1998 though it was not granted legal independence; the ECB became operational in June 1998 and emerged as the most independent bank by virtue of its supranational character. The degree of independence depends on three major factors: independence in personnel matters (appointments of senior officials, term of office, dismissal procedures), independence in financial aspects (financial independence relates to the freedom of the central bank to decide whether government expenditure is financed directly or indirectly via central bank credits; automatic monetisation of deficit subordinates monetary policy to the fiscal policy; if the central bank has a budget of its own it is more independent) and independence in the conduct of monetary policy (policy independence: flexibility given to the bank in formulation and execution of monetary policy; goal independence means the central bank itself can set its own objectives from a broader set; instrument independence means it can choose instruments in order to achieve the pre-specified goals; most central banks have legislative mandates and do not have goal independence as the goals are set by the legislation). In more than two-thirds of central banks surveyed by the BIS at least two or more political bodies were involved in proposing and appointing the candidates; the Federal Reserve Chair is proposed by the President of the US and requires consent of the Congress. The Bundesbank had special provisions that ensured its independence but was also required to support the economic policies of the government. Studies: several studies evaluate the economic implications of central bank independence; these typically estimate quantitative measures of the relative independence and correlate with the average inflation, inflation variability and real economic performance; during the Bretton Woods fixed exchange rate years the industrialised countries that accorded greater legal autonomy to their central banks had experienced lower average inflation; evidence from the 1990s against the backdrop of lower inflation and increasing political commitment to restrain inflation made it harder to identify a correlation between greater central bank independence and lower inflation. Independence is neither a necessity nor a sufficient reason for monetary stability, because independence imparts flexibility and leverage for the central bank role in monetary policy; surveys found central banks independence to be correlated with low inflation rates but it was observed that if independence and low inflation are endogenously determined the correlation does not reveal anything about the direction of causality. A powerful argument that inflation is determined by history and the preferences of a country with causality running from inflation to institutional structure: attempts to impose an independent central bank in a country tolerant of inflation are doomed to fail; but the New Zealand experience: before 1988 the Reserve Bank of New Zealand was one of the least independent central banks in the OECD; after it received a clear mandate in 1988 to fight inflation with a high degree of independence the inflation rate fell from double-digit levels to under 2 per cent; this suggests that the structure of monetary institutions along with the determination to achieve low inflation is a necessary condition to contain inflation. An independent central bank may adopt policies that are conflicting with other policies followed by the government, suggesting the desirability of a coordinated policy approach; one of the major arguments against central bank independence is that it lacks democratic legitimacy, since decisions about interest rate, exchange rates, efficiency of the financial system and other monetary matters are left to the body of unelected officials; however even independent central banks are answerable to the legislature. Independence does not mean absence of communication and the central bank may prefer a regular process of communication and coordination with the government. Preconditions for effective independence of the central bank in itself as a tool to achieve broader macroeconomic goals: central bank should be transparent about its aims; some form of accountability to the legislative body; and maintaining policy credibility with a view to overcoming the time inconsistency problem. The time inconsistency problem arises when the central bank tries to adopt a discretionary monetary policy and reneges its own policy through monetary expansion in a bid to accommodate the wage escalations concluded by trade unions; the options open to the central bank to overcome the time inconsistency problem are (a) the central bank should desist from using the discretionary route to renege their policy to accommodate private perceptions or (b) they should adopt the fixed rule monetary policy which does not permit deviations from the pronounced policy.

Credibility and accountability (courseware): a credible track record of central banks in terms of maintaining low inflation or price stability gains paramount relevance in managing monetary policy; this in a sense shapes and sets the move for adapting public perceptions towards inflation; central banks need to establish reputation for pursuing price stability consistently and persistently; tendencies on the part of central banks to display inconsistent behaviour at different points in time give rise to the time inconsistency or dynamic inconsistency problem; this situation is an outcome of non-adherence to promises made in view of contingencies arising out of pressures on the monetary authorities; if central banks are required to support public debt beyond warranted levels they may not be able to stick to low inflation target; central banks independence in this sense gains utmost relevance for maintaining credibility and price stability; in inflation targeting regimes there is a system of making central bankers responsible for not being able to keep the promises; another alternative is to design policy instruments available to the central bankers such that they are constrained in engineering monetary surprises. If a central bank is viewed as both committed to and effective in maintaining low inflation, then inflation expectations are likely to be lower, eventually leading to movements in prices and wages that are consistent with low and stable inflation; in case central banks do not enjoy credibility in achieving price stability, economic agents tend to incorporate their inflationary expectations in their financial plans, which may result in persistence of inflationary pressures in future rendering central bank action ineffective. Accountability implies bearing responsibility for monetary policy actions; central bank accountability, coupled with autonomy and transparency, facilitates price and financial sector stability, which is conducive to sustainable economic growth; there are few measures of accountability of monetary policy; Briault, Haldane and King constructed a central bank accountability index for fourteen industrialised countries based on parliamentary monitoring, the release of minutes of Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meetings, the publication of monetary policy reports and the existence of an override mechanism; the central bank accountability index reported by Fry and others focuses on accountability with respect to a specific target and public accountability. Accountability is created for the central bank in a democratic set up as a mechanism through which a system of checks and balances is created; there are divergent views as regards the issue of central bank accountability: Nolan and Schaling argued that accountability implies some compromise on central bank independence, while De Haan argued that this conclusion is subjective to the measure of accountability used and is not universally applicable; it was maintained that in the long-term both independence and accountability could co-exist; in a democratic set up the conduct of central bank policy should elicit political support, else the central bank may sooner or later be over-ridden; even the most independent central bank like the Federal Reserve is accountable in the sense that the Chairman of the US Fed has to testify before the Congress periodically. Ways of ensuring accountability: clearly specifying the main goals (it is sometimes argued that accountability is facilitated by setting up a single objective, typically price stability, which is explicitly stated numerically; it is also argued that fixing a strict inflation target to the exclusion of all other equally important targets like output growth is not a desirable approach); reappointment process for the central banker; and in the Bank of England Act operational independence and accountability are combined: if the inflation target is missed by more than one percentage point, either in the direction of overshooting or undershooting, the Governor, on behalf of the Monetary Policy Committee, is required to write an open letter to the Chancellor explaining the causes behind the overshooting or undershooting, the time it would take for the policies to impact on inflation and bring it back to the targeted level; the MPC members are collectively responsible and individually responsible and accountable to the Court of Directors; the MPC regularly publishes a quarterly inflation report and inflation forecasts. Central banks have adopted certain mechanisms to ensure accountability: review of a central bank decisions, budget, expenditures and transparency in operating procedures and the monetary policy making process; the Governor of the central bank testifies before the Congress or parliament in a number of countries; in some countries a publicly appointed supervisory board, not the government, approves the central bank operational budget; the BIS and the IMF norms relating to data dissemination also contribute to the accountability; the publication of the annual reports, inflation reports and the proceedings or minutes of monetary policy committee meetings are important methods to ensure accountability. Three types of best practices that enhance transparency: publication of official reports that analyse economic conditions; publication of forecasts of key variables (inflation, output) and their central forecast as well as risks; and explaining the reasons for central bank decisions and various contingencies under consideration.

Transparency in central bank operations (courseware): transparency in the case of central banks can be defined as the absence of asymmetric information between monetary policy makers and other economic agents with a view to reducing the uncertainty. The need for transparency has emanated from several developments in recent years: episodes of financial crises resulting from information asymmetries, growing integration of financial markets, the need for enhanced autonomy as well as accountability of central banks, and the emphasis on financial stability have necessitated increased transparency on the part of central banks and market participants. Transparency is the offshoot of accountability in many ways; detailed discussion of the decisions and monetary policy operations is essential as central banks act as agents in a principal-agent relationship vis-a-vis society at large and in most cases they have been granted independent status in order to better fulfil their main mandate; transparency is a secondary but an important objective of the central bank; this is because the accountability of the central bank is centred on the bank fulfilling its primary objective relating to monetary policy. The stability of financial system could be achieved only when institutions and market players take informed decisions; adequate disclosure acts as a deterrent to discretionary monetary policy, time inconsistency and excessive risk taking; it also enables the market participants to be aware of the costs and commitments in financial contracts; monetary and financial policies can be made more effective if the public knows and understands the goals and instruments of policy and if central banks and financial agencies make a credible commitment towards achieving them. International initiatives: the efforts first became prominent at the 1995 Halifax Summit of the G-7 countries; the efforts received greater thrust in the aftermath of the East Asian crisis; in April 1998 finance ministers and central bank Governors met in Washington and working groups were set up in three areas: enhancing transparency and accountability; strengthening domestic financial systems; and managing international financial crisis. The International Monetary Fund formulated a Code of Good Practices on Transparency in Monetary and Financial Policies in March 2000, known as the ELRIC framework: ELRIC stands for five areas, viz., external audit mechanism, legal structure and independence, financial reporting, internal audit mechanism and a system of internal control; the ELRIC framework employs International Financial Reporting Standards, International Standards on Auditing, guidelines promulgated by the Institute of Internal Auditors and the IMF Data Dissemination Standards as benchmarks; the safeguard assessment is a diagnostic exercise, carried out by the IMF, to assess these five key areas of control and governance of a central bank; the safeguards assessment generates a report to identify vulnerabilities in the operations of a central bank and offers recommendations to mitigate them. Key international standards and codes (Box 3.1): the idea of application of standards was triggered after the Mexican crisis of 1994; the expression standards and codes is used to include transparency practices in macro policy, core principles relating to regulatory and supervisory systems and market infrastructure; the Task Force on Implementation of Standards (chaired by Mr Andrew Sheng), constituted by the Financial Stability Forum (FSF), favoured 12 as the key standards; the Reserve Bank of India was represented on the Task Force; the IMFC adopted it. The 12 key standards: monetary and financial policy transparency (Code of Good Practices on Transparency in Monetary and Financial Policies, IMF); fiscal policy transparency (Code of Good Practices on Fiscal Transparency, IMF); data dissemination (Special Data Dissemination Standard / General Data Dissemination Standard, IMF); insolvency (Principles and Guidelines on Effective Insolvency and Creditor Rights System, World Bank); corporate governance (Principles of Corporate Governance, OECD); accounting (International Accounting Standards, IASB); auditing (International Standards on Auditing, IFAC); payment and settlement (Core Principles for Systemically Important Financial Institutions (SIFIs), CPSS-BIS); market integrity (Forty Recommendations of the Financial Action Task Force on Money Laundering, FATF-OECD); banking supervision (Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision, BCBS); and insurance supervision (Insurance Core Principles, IAIS). The need for transparency and communication increases in line with the level of discretion used in the formulation of monetary policy; the IMF identified the data to be disseminated and the time-frame; publication of objective data is generally perceived as a highly desirable objective; central bank credibility plays an important role in steering the perceptions of the public; it is an intangible asset; credibility is difficult to quantify, and establishing empirical evidence in regard to the relationship between central bank independence, credibility and lower inflation is difficult, but credibility can be inferred from the central bank track record in achieving its strong commitment to price stability.

Conflict with fiscal policies (courseware): effective coordination between the central bank, which formulates monetary policy, and the government, responsible for fiscal policy, is required for achieving the common set of macroeconomic objectives. Historical background: the early central banks (like those in Sweden and England), unlike the present day ones, were set up to support the governments in financing their budgetary gaps, facilitated by legislation granting monopoly rights of issuing currency to the central banks; over time the privileged position of the central bank, being the monopoly issuer of currency and simultaneously acting as the banker to the government, resulted in a situation where the owner of the central bank (the government) became its principal debtor; governments became prone to depend heavily on central bank advances or limits for their financing requirements; such unmitigated access resulted in erosion of the value of currency issued by the central banks; the role of the central bank being the banker to the government hindered its principal objective of maintaining monetary stability; therein lies the genesis of the conflict of monetary policy objectives with its role of being the banker to the government. Theoretical underpinnings: Keynes brought about a revolution in macroeconomic thinking by constructing a monetary theory around a fully developed financial system with the central bank at its centre; Keynes integrated the monetary and real sectors of the economy by emphasising the inter-linkage between the rate of interest and the level of investment; in the first two decades after the Second World War the Keynesian tenet took the position that spending decisions of consumers and firms move largely independent of asset rates of return, so fiscal policy came to the central stage; the ascendancy of fiscal policy during this period was partly due to the Great Depression and post-war reconstruction. The Keynesian tenets were called into question by events in the early 1970s: breakdown of the fixed exchange rate system, the first OPEC oil shock, bad harvests and crop failure combined with the aftermath of the Vietnam War, which led to acceleration in inflation and high unemployment (stagflation); subsequent analysis showed that there is essentially no long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment. During the 1970s the new-classical economists, assuming rational expectations of market participants and a market-clearing approach without rigidity, argued that anticipated policy measures do not matter and that only unanticipated policy can have any real, but temporary, impact; to avoid generating surprises stabilisation policy should not be discretionary but should be rule based; rule based monetary and fiscal policy was recommended; the rational expectations paradigm substantially influenced theory and the conduct of future monetary policy; Keynesian economists demonstrated that, even with assumption of rational expectations, anticipated policy measures can have real effects provided the market clearing assumption was relaxed; further evidence underscored that fiscal policy is not sufficiently agile to be effective in a stabilisation role as it is heavily influenced by exogenous political considerations; fiscal policy represents merely another demand shock to be countered by monetary policy; as a result monetary policy gained ascendancy necessitating, in many cases, institutional changes like the creation of independent central banks to counter fiscally profligate governments; such thinking largely influenced the functioning of the erstwhile German Bundesbank and laid the foundation for the European Central Bank. During the 1980s the theory of stabilisation policy received a further boost through the application of game theory: non-cooperative behaviour in the form of frictions between the two arms of economic policy (fiscal and monetary) resulted in sub-optimal outcomes for society; greater monetary fiscal coordination has been emphasised upon since the mid-1980s. Global experience: governments have borrowed heavily from central banks for financing colonial expansion, wars and for building up the war ravaged economies during the post-World War II period; deficit financing did not yield inflationary expectations along with high levels of capacity utilisation; fiscal policy-led recovery quickly hit a roadblock in the wake of supply shocks; the stagflation in the 1970s is attributed to these factors; accordingly governments were bestowed with the responsibility of enhancing economic growth, and central banks were mandated to ensure monetary stability; both objectives are desirable; better coordination between the two arms (fiscal and monetary) has been emphasised since the mid-1980s. Governments in a number of countries, in recent years, have increasingly disciplined themselves by enacting fiscal responsibility legislations encompassing, inter alia, placing restrictions on central bank accommodation and setting of borrowing limits or ceilings, thus rendering monetary policy more flexible and independent for stabilising inflation; some countries which had a history of hyper-inflation enacted legislations on central bank autonomy too. Developing and emerging economies: central banks have to take active interest in the fiscal position because the size of the deficit and the mode of financing will influence interest rates and prices (the two most important key variables that all central banks assiduously track); in most countries central banks perform the monopoly of note issue function and in pursuing this objective they also seek to ensure price stability; central banks also seek to influence employment and output; a low rate of interest encourages bank credit and promotes investment; reducing the reserve ratio could encourage bank expansion; in EMEs, the dominant financing of public debt takes place through domestic financing of fiscal deficits; the option of foreign financing of public debt has been found to be very limited in EMEs because the government papers are not traded or their rating in international markets is low; the financing of deficits by the central bank may eventually lead to a debt trap in the sense that the government resorts to borrowing year after year, the repayment of principal and payment of interest may have to be made on the accumulated debt; the government may have to borrow more and more every year; there is need to break the debt trap which may eventually escalate the inflationary pressures. An alternative option for the government to finance its deficit would be to access financial markets: such market borrowing could occur through the issuance and sale of treasury bills and bonds of a wide variety of maturities; critics contend that the use of this alternative policy option is beset with the problem of crowding out of private investment, i.e., funds available for financing of private investment are in effect transferred for the government to finance the deficit and consequently the funds available for financing of private investment would be reduced; the critics point out that the reduction in private investment would adversely affect the growth process. Central banks hold stocks of government securities as part of managing public debt; these securities serve as a backing for currency and as an instrument of monetary control for central bank; the central bank conducts open market operations and influences the liquidity in the system; as government absorbs a larger chunk of liquidity in the system there would be a pressure on the availability of funds in the economy: (a) since banks and financial institutions would absorb these securities, they will be constrained in conducting their lending operations; (b) crowding out effect as depletion of funds may lead to pressure on demand for funds in the market and consequently push up the rate of interest. Modes of absorption of government borrowing by central banks through primary dealers: the government announces its targeted level of borrowing at the beginning of every year in its budget document; the central bank, by virtue of its role as manager of public debt, implements the market borrowing programme; participants in the Market Borrowing Programme (MBP) are (a) RBI (b) commercial banks (c) other financial institutions (d) individuals and (e) Primary Dealers; primary dealers are registered entities with the RBI and play role of market makers in respect of the government securities; they also act as underwriters for the devolved portion of the government securities issued under the government borrowing programme; in case the other market participants are unable to absorb the offered securities/bonds even at the announced rates, the central bank would then be asking primary dealers (PDs), as underwriters to invest in the unabsorbed portion of securities; thus the central bank completes the target set by the Government; the process of absorption of government securities by the PDs is usually termed as devolvement; alternatively, many prefer to opt for private placement of government securities for subsequent offloading in the market; devolvement occurs when central banks are not in a position to gauge the liquidity in the economy appropriately or due to the portfolio behaviour of banks, central banks are unable to offload the securities in the market. Direct monetisation by absorbing the securities, be they bonds or treasury bills, offered by governments at a certain interest rate is rarely preferred by central banks; in India direct monetisation existed since the mid-fifties and lasted till the end of March 1997 (the practice of ad hoc Treasury Bills); private placement of government securities with central banks came into existence only since the second half of the 1990s; private placement, theoretically speaking, is a form of monetisation in that the securities are first absorbed by the central bank on a temporary basis to provide temporary support to government financing needs. Absorption of government borrowing by central banks by way of private placements has implications for the economy: such private placements could push up commodity prices on the expectations of fuelling aggregate demand in the short run; in order to minimise or smoothen the adverse influences of private placements central banks generally try to offload the private placements as quickly as they can; this is achieved by central banks injecting liquidity through liberal refinancing at competitive interest rates, or through absorption of foreign exchange from the market or through repo operations; the consequent increase in market liquidity would help the central banks to reduce the possibility of its accepting private placement or to offload the privately placed securities on to the credit markets. But all these measures would lead to an increase in aggregate demand and rise in prices; offloading privately placed securities at a later date, however, may not always succeed as banks could refuse to absorb government securities in periods of economic buoyancy and if the expected yield rates on bonds are not attractive or market related. In many EMEs the secondary market for government securities is not well developed, sufficiently large and deep enough; therefore, banks may not be prepared to face the liquidity risks by holding government securities that would be far in excess of the statutory liquidity requirements; banks may prefer to lend rather than invest in government securities as the return on lending may be higher than on government securities. Central banks in EMEs will be in a most difficult position if they are to manage large public borrowing during periods of economic down-turn and particularly in a scenario of public expenditures being unproductive; in such circumstances central banks may need to inject huge liquidity into the system if the interest servicing costs are to be kept low; such a strategy would eventually lead to increase in prices since the economy faces a situation of too much money chasing too few goods. The concerted monetary-fiscal action for accommodating the fiscal need of lowering the interest servicing costs would water down the monetary discipline and harm the overall economic performance in the medium term.

Monetary policy and debt management: the Indian experience and separation of debt management (courseware): as early as 1957 the Reserve Bank of India had raised concerns over its accommodation of the government through ad hoc Treasury Bills when it drew the attention of the Government to the fact that the creation of ad hoc Treasury Bills to maintain the Government closing balance each week had become a merely mechanical process with no checks on the Government ability to spend without regard to the available resources; according to the Reserve Bank the Bank is not really in a position to discharge the responsibility vested in it by statute of regulating the issue of banknotes with a view to securing monetary stability in India (Balachandran, 1998). Ad hoc Treasury Bills in India (Box 3.2): the origin of ad hoc Treasury Bills in India dated back to World War II when they were issued by the Government of India to the Reserve Bank mainly in connection with the temporary financing of sterling debt repatriation; ad hoc Treasury Bills were also issued in 1948-49 to replace sterling securities transferred to the UK Government in terms of the sterling balance agreement of 1948; the operational arrangement in March 1955 enabled automatic creation of ad hoc Treasury Bills to restore Central Government cash balance to the minimum stipulated level whenever there was excess cash drawn down; the practice of funding (consolidation of public debt by issue of funded or dated securities in place of floating debt such as treasury bills and ways and means advances) was compounded as large amounts of ad hocs were rolled over and from 1982 were converted into undated non-marketable special securities carrying a discount rate of 4.6 per cent; the conversion of the outstanding ad hoc Treasury bills into dated securities; as at end-March 1994 and later, the outstanding amount of special securities held by the Reserve Bank; the outstanding amount of ad hoc Treasury Bills converted to special securities as at end-March 1997 (the figures are as given in the Reserve Bank reports and are not reproduced). Transition from automatic monetisation to Ways and Means Advances (Box 3.3): monetary policy had to contend with the imperatives of automatic monetisation through accommodating Government of India ad hoc Treasury Bills up to March 1997; to check this unbridled automatic monetisation of Government deficits, the First Supplemental Agreement between the Reserve Bank and the Government of India on 9 September 1994 set out a system of limits for creation of ad hocs during the three-year period 1994-95 to 1996-97 before being completely phased out from April 1997; on 6 March 1997 the Supplemental Agreement between the Central Government and the Reserve Bank completely phased out the ad hoc Treasury Bills by end-March 1997 by funding ad hoc Treasury Bills as on end-March 1997 into special securities at 4.6 per cent on 1 April 1997, replaced by a system of Ways and Means Advances (WMA) commencing 1 April 1997; the WMA system provides for extending short-term advances to the Government that are repayable within a period of three months; and in order to smoothen the transition the proportion of auction 91-day Treasury Bills was increased. The Reserve Bank can trigger fresh floatation of Government securities whenever 75 per cent of the WMA limit is reached; the Reserve Bank as a banker to government provides overdraft where WMA limit is exceeded at an interest rate higher than that of the WMA. Episodes of conflict: in the 1960s during inflationary pressures the Reserve Bank adopted measures to tighten monetary policy by imposing an incremental CRR in 1960 though it wanted to raise the Bank Rate; it was not till 1963 that the Reserve Bank could raise Bank Rate by 50 basis points; thus the freedom to choose the monetary tool was to some extent compromised; during 1960-66 the Reserve Bank raised its Bank Rate from 4 per cent to 6 per cent and initiated a series of measures to restrict accommodation to banks; to stabilise market conditions, the Reserve Bank became a net purchaser of government securities through its OMOs, thereby infusing liquidity. Separation of debt management from monetary management: a proposal has been mooted in recent years for assigning the debt management function to a separate entity that would coordinate its actions with the central bank for the purposes of timing and economising on the costs of borrowing; the theoretical underpinning is that the government would fully fund its deficit by borrowing from the public at market rates of interest and completely free the central bank from debt management responsibility; the government would (a) enable the central bank to pursue its price stability objective without getting diverted in issues of debt management, and (b) endeavour to work out strategies to minimise borrowing costs. The government would take decisions on: (i) the size of the issue, (ii) the proportions of the issue in terms of bonds, treasury bills and different variants such as indexed bonds, (iii) the proportions of the issue in terms of home currency and in terms of denominated foreign currencies where foreign currency borrowing is permitted, (iv) the timing of the issues, as well as the maturity patterns of issues, and the amount of coupons. A separate entity does not mean that it would never consult with the market participants, including the central bank; the central bank would be in a unique position to give advice to the separate debt management entity on the size and timing of the issue as it constantly keeps track of liquidity conditions in the economy; as a banker to the government, the central bank would continue to conduct the processing of tenders for bonds and bills and manage the registry; in most cases the central bank would also provide the clearance and settlement services in respect of the government securities. New Zealand established a separate government office to manage government debt in the late 1980s and has achieved considerable success in ensuring that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand has autonomy in monetary policy making; Ireland, Sweden, Australia and the United Kingdom have also established separate sovereign debt management units; there are other countries such as Austria, Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Hungary, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and the United States that have evolved sophisticated units responsible for public debt management. Another important reason that calls for separation of debt management from monetary management is that if both functions are located in a single body, it is likely that monetary policy may be so managed as to benefit debt management operations, and this is an insider information problem; in view of this possibility, even if a separate entity for debt management is not created, it is essential to clearly define and allocate responsibilities for debt management and monetary management separately so that accountability for respective functions are established; EMEs could develop suitable legislation and institutional mechanisms for smooth implementation of both functional areas.

payload.title: Autonomy and independence of a central bank
payload.core_explanation_md:
**History:** central banks began as **private** institutions, **independent of government** until the **Second World War**; around WWII **Germany, France, England, Japan, Italy and Sweden** subordinated them to governments; experience since has shown banks **work best when autonomous** and that **low inflation** is more attainable.

**Revival of interest** came from **reforms in planned economies**, the new **European Central Bank (ECB)** and the need for **price stability** amid **cross border capital flows**.

**Arguments for independence:** governments are **myopic** and drift to **inflationary policy** for short-run gains; the more the bank **supports public debt**, the more **pressure on liquidity management**; an independent bank can take the **long view**.

**Recent milestones (courseware):** **Bank of England** legally independent in **June 1998**; **Bank of Japan** gained **operational (not legal) independence in April 1998**; **ECB** operational in **June 1998** and the **most independent** because it is **supranational**.

**Three dimensions of independence:**

| Dimension | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Personnel** | Appointment of officials, **term of office**, **dismissal rules**; in **over two-thirds** of banks surveyed by the BIS at least **two political bodies** were involved in proposing and appointing |
| **Financial** | Freedom from **automatic monetisation** of deficits; the **bank's own budget** |
| **Policy** | **Goal independence** (bank sets its own goals) vs **instrument independence** (bank chooses instruments for goals set by law) — most banks have **instrument but not goal independence** |

**Evidence:** studies link independence with **lower average inflation**, especially under **Bretton Woods**; in the **1990s** the link was **harder to see**; the **correlation may be endogenous**; **New Zealand** (**independence and a clear mandate in 1988**) took inflation from **double digits to under 2 per cent**. **Critics:** it lacks **democratic legitimacy**; but banks stay **answerable to the legislature**.

**Preconditions:** **transparency about aims**, **accountability to the legislature** and **credibility to overcome time inconsistency**. **Time inconsistency** arises when the bank **abandons its own policy** (for example expanding money to **accommodate wage settlements**); the cures are **no discretionary reneging** or a **fixed rule**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Independence works best when paired with transparency and accountability.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The central bank sets its own objectives rather than having them set by law.

payload.title: Credibility and accountability of a central bank
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Credibility:** a **track record** of low inflation shapes **public expectations**; if people trust the bank, **inflation expectations stay low** and **prices and wages follow**; if not, they **build inflation into their plans** and policy becomes **ineffective**. **Time (dynamic) inconsistency** erodes credibility when the bank **fails to stick to its promises** under **pressure to support public debt**. Remedies: **independence**, **inflation targeting regimes** that **hold the central bank responsible** for missing targets, and **instruments that limit surprises**.

**Accountability** means **responsibility for policy actions**; together with **autonomy and transparency** it supports **price and financial sector stability**. Measures: the **Briault, Haldane and King index** (parliamentary monitoring, **minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee**, **policy reports**, an **override mechanism**) and the **Fry index** (accountability for a **specific target** and **public accountability**). **Nolan and Schaling:** accountability implies **some compromise** of independence; **De Haan:** that depends on the **measure**; in the long run both **can co-exist**. Even the **Fed** is accountable: the **Chair testifies to Congress**.

**Ways to ensure accountability:** **clear goals** (a **single numerical price stability objective** helps, but excluding all other goals is **not desirable**); a **reappointment process**; reviews of **decisions, budget and spending**; **testimony to the legislature**; a **supervisory board** approving the bank's **budget**; and **publication** of **annual reports, inflation reports and MPC minutes**.

**Bank of England example:** if inflation misses the target by **more than one percentage point** in either direction, the **Governor (for the MPC)** must **write an open letter to the Chancellor**, explaining the cause and how long it will take to **return to target**; the MPC **publishes a quarterly inflation report**.

**Transparency best practices:** **official reports** analysing the economy, **forecasts of key variables with risks**, and **reasons for decisions**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Accountability is the democratic counterpart of independence.

self_check.prompt_text: According to the courseware, in what situation must the Bank of England's Governor write an open letter to the Chancellor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: When inflation misses the target by more than one percentage point, above or below.

payload.title: Transparency and key international standards and codes
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Definition:** transparency is the **absence of asymmetric information** between policy makers and other agents, **reducing uncertainty**. It is needed because of **financial crises caused by information gaps**, **integrated markets**, **greater autonomy and accountability** and the **stress on financial stability**. It is a **secondary but important objective**: the bank is an **agent** answerable to the public (**principal-agent** relationship). **Disclosure** deters **discretionary policy**, **time inconsistency** and **excess risk taking**, and **policy works better** when the public **knows what the goals and instruments are**.

**International initiatives:** began at the **1995 Halifax Summit (G-7)**; in **April 1998**, in the wake of the **East Asian crisis**, finance ministers and central bank Governors set up **three working groups**: **transparency and accountability**, **strengthening domestic financial systems**, **managing international financial crisis**.

**IMF Code of Good Practices on Transparency in Monetary and Financial Policies (March 2000)** and the **ELRIC** framework (**E**xternal audit mechanism, **L**egal structure and independence, financial **R**eporting, **I**nternal audit mechanism and a system of internal **C**ontrol); the IMF **safeguards assessment** is a **diagnostic** of these five areas.

**Twelve key standards (after the 1994 Mexican crisis, Task Force chaired by Andrew Sheng):**

| Area | Standard | Body |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monetary and financial policy transparency | **Code of Good Practices** | **IMF** |
| Fiscal transparency | **Code of Good Practices on Fiscal Transparency** | **IMF** |
| Data dissemination | **SDDS / GDDS** | **IMF** |
| Insolvency | **Principles and Guidelines on Effective Insolvency and Creditor Rights System** | **World Bank** |
| Corporate governance | **Principles of Corporate Governance** | **OECD** |
| Accounting | **International Accounting Standards** | **IASB** |
| Auditing | **International Standards on Auditing** | **IFAC** |
| Payment and settlement | **Core Principles for Systemically Important Payment Systems** | **CPSS-BIS** |
| Market integrity | **Forty Recommendations (money laundering)** | **FATF-OECD** |
| Banking supervision | **Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision** | **BCBS** |
| Insurance supervision | **Insurance Core Principles** | **IAIS** |

**Credibility** is an **intangible asset**, hard to measure, but shown by a **track record** of achieving **price stability**.

payload.title: Conflict with fiscal policy: history, theory and global experience
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Origin of conflict:** early central banks were set up to **finance governments**; with **note issue monopoly** and the role of **government banker**, the **owner (government) became the bank's principal debtor**; **unmitigated access** to central bank credit **eroded the currency's value** and hindered **monetary stability**.

**Theory:**

- **Keynes** linked money and the real sector through **interest rate and investment**; for two decades after WWII **fiscal policy** took centre stage (Depression, reconstruction).
- The **1970s** (collapse of fixed exchange rates, **oil shock**, bad harvests, Vietnam war) produced **stagflation**: **no long-run trade-off** between inflation and unemployment.
- **New-classical economists** (**rational expectations**, market clearing): **only unanticipated policy has real effects, and only temporarily**; prefer **rules** over **discretion**.
- **Keynesians** replied that anticipated policy can matter if markets do not clear; **fiscal policy** is **not agile** (political influence) and amounts to **another demand shock** monetary policy must offset; so **independent central banks** (the **Bundesbank**, later the **ECB**) were favoured.
- **Game theory (1980s):** **non-cooperation** between fiscal and monetary authorities gives **sub-optimal outcomes**; **coordination** stressed since the **mid-1980s**.

**Fiscal responsibility legislation** (limits on central bank accommodation and borrowing ceilings) frees monetary policy; some countries with **hyperinflation** history legislated **central bank autonomy**.

**Emerging economies:** central banks watch the **fiscal position** because **deficit size and financing** drive **interest rates and prices**; **foreign financing** of public debt is **limited**, so **domestic financing** dominates; deficit financing by the central bank risks a **debt trap** (borrowing to repay earlier debt); **market borrowing** instead risks **crowding out private investment**; central banks hold government securities as **backing for currency** and for **OMOs**; large government absorption of liquidity **constrains bank lending** and **pushes up interest rates**.

**Market borrowing programme and primary dealers (PDs):** the Government announces its **annual borrowing** in the budget; participants: **RBI, commercial banks, other financial institutions, individuals and PDs**. **PDs** are **registered market makers** and **underwriters**; the unsubscribed portion that falls to them is **devolvement**. **Private placement** with the central bank is a **temporary form of monetisation**; **direct monetisation** (India: **ad hoc Treasury Bills from the mid-1950s to March 1997**) is rarely preferred. The central bank tries to **offload privately placed securities quickly** (liquidity injection through **refinancing, foreign exchange absorption or repos**), though that adds to demand and prices. In **EMEs** the **secondary market is thin**, so banks prefer **lending** to holding securities above the **SLR**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Coordination and legal limits on central bank financing are the practical answers to the conflict.

payload.title: Indian experience with debt management and separation of debt management
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Concern in 1957:** the Reserve Bank warned that creation of **ad hoc Treasury Bills** to keep the Government's **weekly closing balance** had become a **mechanical process** with **no check on spending**, undermining its **statutory duty** to secure **monetary stability**.

**Ad hoc Treasury Bills:** originated in **World War II** (financing **sterling debt repatriation**), used again in **1948-49** for the **sterling balance agreement**; from **March 1955** an arrangement **automatically** created them to restore the Government's cash balance; they were **funded** into **undated special securities at 4.6 per cent from 1982**.

**Ending automatic monetisation:**

- **9 September 1994** First Supplemental Agreement: **limits on ad hocs** during **1994-95 to 1996-97**, then **phase out from April 1997**.
- **6 March 1997** Supplemental Agreement: **ad hocs completely phased out**; replaced from **1 April 1997** by **Ways and Means Advances (WMA)**: **short-term advances repayable within three months**.
- The Reserve Bank can **float fresh government securities** when **75 per cent of the WMA limit** is reached; **overdraft** beyond the limit carries an **interest rate higher than WMA**.

**1960s conflicts:** the Reserve Bank used an **incremental CRR in 1960** because it could not raise the **Bank Rate**; the Bank Rate moved **4 to 6 per cent in 1960-66**; it became a **net purchaser of government securities** to steady markets.

**Separating debt management from monetary policy:** the Government would **fully fund the deficit from the public at market rates**, **taking debt management out of the central bank**; it would decide **size, instruments (bonds, bills, indexed), currency, timing, maturity and coupon**; the central bank would still **advise on size and timing** (it tracks liquidity), **process tenders**, **maintain the registry** and provide **clearing and settlement**. **New Zealand** set up a separate office in the **late 1980s**; **Ireland, Sweden, Australia and the UK** followed. Reasons for separation: avoid an **insider information problem** (monetary policy tailored to help debt operations) and keep **accountability** clear; if not separated, **allocate and define responsibilities separately**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: India replaced automatic monetisation with a limited, temporary facility, a clear policy decision to protect monetary control.
